q: How long did the 1621 Plymouth harvest feast—often called the 'First Thanksgiving'—actually last?
quote: The autumn 1621 celebration between the Plymouth colonists and the Wampanoag people lasted three full days!

q: Which meat was definitely documented on the table at the 1621 feast by Pilgrim chronicler Edward Winslow?
quote: Wampanoag leader Massasoit and his men brought five deer (venison) as a gift to share at the three-day feast.

q: Which everyday eating utensil was completely missing from the 1621 Plymouth Thanksgiving table?
quote: The Pilgrims ate with knives, spoons, and their fingers! Table forks didn't become common in America until the 1700s.

q: Who spent 36 years writing letters to presidents—and also wrote 'Mary Had a Little Lamb'—convincing Abraham Lincoln to make Thanksgiving a national holiday in 1863?
quote: Magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for 36 years before President Lincoln proclaimed Thanksgiving a national holiday in October 1863.

q: Why did President Franklin D. Roosevelt briefly move Thanksgiving one week earlier in 1939—a controversy nicknamed 'Franksgiving'?
a: To lengthen the Christmas shopping season during the Great Depression
To line up with the Army-Navy football game
quote: Retailers begged FDR for extra holiday shopping days during the Great Depression. After half the country refused to switch dates, Congress permanently fixed Thanksgiving as the fourth Thursday of November in 1941.

q: Which Founding Father praised the wild turkey in a letter to his daughter as a 'much more respectable Bird' than the bald eagle?
quote: In a 1784 letter to his daughter Sarah, Benjamin Franklin joked that the bald eagle had 'bad moral character' while the turkey was a 'Bird of Courage.'

q: What is the proper name for the long, fleshy red appendage that hangs down over a turkey's beak?
quote: The flap hanging over the beak is the snood! (The red skin under the chin and neck is the wattle.)

q: Which turkeys actually make the famous 'gobble, gobble' sound?
quote: Only male turkeys (called toms or gobblers) gobble! Female turkeys (hens) communicate with clicks, purrs, and yelps.

q: How fast can a wild turkey fly in short bursts when escaping danger?
a: Wild turkeys cannot fly at all
quote: While heavy domestic farm turkeys can't fly, wild turkeys can sprint 20 mph on land and fly up to 55 mph in short bursts!

q: Which U.S. President made the White House turkey pardon an official annual tradition in 1989, assuring the bird it would 'not end up on anyone's dinner table'?
quote: Though earlier presidents occasionally spared gift turkeys, George H.W. Bush turned the formal 'presidential pardon' into a permanent annual ceremony in 1989.

q: How did the giant 1953 frozen turkey surplus at Swanson (260 tons of leftover birds sitting in refrigerated train cars!) change American dining?
a: It led to the invention of the frozen TV Dinner
It created the first canned turkey soup
It started the first turkey fast-food chain
It inspired the invention of the microwave oven
quote: Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas packed the extra turkey with cornbread dressing, peas, and sweet potatoes on aluminum trays inspired by airline meals—creating the very first TV Dinner!

q: Why are ripe cranberries sometimes nicknamed 'bounceberries' by cranberry farmers?
a: They bounce off water when harvested
Fresh, unbruised cranberries bounce like rubber balls because of tiny air pockets inside
They grow on springy vines that snap back when picked
They pop and bounce out of the pan when boiled
quote: Healthy cranberries have four little air chambers inside—farmers even use mechanical 'bounce-board' separators that make fresh berries jump over wooden barriers!

q: Who created the iconic Green Bean Casserole recipe in 1955 using canned green beans, cream of mushroom soup, and crispy fried onions?
a: Dorcas Reilly at the Campbell Soup Company
quote: Home economist Dorcas Reilly invented the dish in Campbell's test kitchen in 1955 using ingredients most American pantries already had on hand.

q: Which amino acid in turkey is famous for getting blamed for post-Thanksgiving naps—even though chicken and cheddar cheese actually contain just as much or more of it?
quote: Turkey does contain L-tryptophan, but nutritionists say the real culprit behind the Thanksgiving food coma is eating a huge load of carbohydrates and dessert all at once!

q: What did the pop-up plastic turkey timer (invented in the 1960s) originally use inside its tip to release the spring when the turkey reached ~180°F?
a: A tiny bead of soft metal solder that melts at roasting temperature
quote: Inside a pop-up timer, a spring-loaded stem is held down by a drop of food-safe soft metal alloy (or paraffin wax in newer models) that melts right around 180°F!

q: Instead of giant helium balloons, what marched down the streets of New York City in the very first Macy's parade in 1924?
a: Live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo
100 Broadway tap dancers dressed as turkeys
quote: The 1924 Macy's parade (originally called the Macy's Christmas Parade!) featured bears, elephants, camels, and monkeys borrowed from the Central Park Zoo.

q: Which cartoon character became the first giant helium balloon in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1927?
quote: Felix the Cat debuted in 1927 as the parade's first giant balloon (initially filled with air, before helium was used the following year).

q: Which iconic character holds the all-time record for appearing as the most different balloon designs (8 versions and over 40 flights!) in Macy's Parade history?
quote: Snoopy first flew in 1968 as an aviator and has returned in eight different balloon designs—including an astronaut and Beagle Scout!

q: Which two NFL teams have hosted a Thanksgiving Day football game almost every single year for decades?
a: Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears
New England Patriots and New York Giants
quote: The Detroit Lions started hosting on Thanksgiving in 1934, and the Dallas Cowboys joined as the second annual Thanksgiving host in 1966.

q: What unusual three-bird roast did legendary football broadcaster John Madden make famous by awarding its legs to NFL Thanksgiving game MVPs?
a: The Turducken (a chicken inside a duck inside a turkey)
quote: John Madden loved carving a six-legged Turducken (deboned chicken stuffed into a deboned duck stuffed into a deboned turkey) live on the Thanksgiving broadcast!

q: Why is the busiest shopping Friday after Thanksgiving called 'Black Friday'—before retailers later spun it as the day stores go 'into the black'?
a: 1950s Philadelphia police used it to describe the chaotic traffic jams and crowds before the Army-Navy game
Department stores used to dim their window lights until 6:00 a.m.
Newspapers printed their Friday sale ads on black paper
Coal delivery trucks blocked downtown streets every November
quote: Philadelphia police officers coined 'Black Friday' in the 1950s because every officer had to work 12-hour shifts handling suburban shoppers and Army-Navy football crowds.

q: According to plumbers across the United States, what do they nickname the day after Thanksgiving—their single busiest emergency call day of the year?
quote: Roto-Rooter and plumbers nationwide call the day after Thanksgiving 'Brown Friday'—calls jump by over 50% thanks to turkey grease, potato peels, and extra houseguests!

q: The familiar melody of which winter holiday song was originally written in 1857 by James Lord Pierpont for a Sunday school Thanksgiving program?
quote: 'Jingle Bells' (originally titled 'The One Horse Open Sleigh') was written for a Thanksgiving church concert in Savannah/Medford and doesn't mention Christmas once!

q: In the classic 1973 TV special 'A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving,' what four-item feast do Snoopy and Linus prepare for the gang at the ping-pong table?
a: Buttered toast, popcorn, pretzel sticks, and jelly beans
Peanut butter sandwiches, apple slices, marshmallows, and hot cocoa
Canned cranberry sauce, saltine crackers, cheese cubes, and pie
Waffles, chocolate chips, potato chips, and root beer
quote: Peppermint Patty is outraged when Snoopy serves buttered toast, popcorn, pretzel sticks, and jelly beans (plus an ice cream sundae)—before Marcie reminds her what Thanksgiving is really about!

q: When does Canada celebrate its national Thanksgiving holiday each year?
quote: Because Canada is farther north, its harvest season arrives earlier—so Canadian Thanksgiving is celebrated on the second Monday of October!

q: Which Native American from the Patuxet tribe spoke English, taught the Pilgrims how to plant corn with fish fertilizer, and served as interpreter at the 1621 feast?
quote: Tisquantum (Squanto) had learned English during earlier voyages to Europe and helped broker peace between the Plymouth colonists and Wampanoag chief Massasoit.

q: About how many Wampanoag guests joined the 53 surviving Plymouth colonists at the three-day 1621 harvest feast?
quote: Wampanoag leader Massasoit arrived with roughly 90 men—nearly double the number of surviving Mayflower colonists—and stayed for three days!

q: Why was there almost certainly no pumpkin pie or bread stuffing at the 1621 Plymouth feast?
a: Pumpkins had not been discovered in North America yet
English law forbade eating dessert on feast days
The Pilgrims had run out of sugar and wheat flour and had no oven for baking pastries
All of their pumpkins had frozen in an October blizzard
quote: The Mayflower's flour and sugar stores had dwindled, so the colonists likely hollowed out pumpkins and roasted them with honey, spices, or milk over open fires instead of baking crusted pies.

q: Before crossing the Atlantic on the Mayflower, in which Dutch city did many of the Pilgrims live for over a decade—where an annual October 3rd 'Leidens Ontzet' thanksgiving feast inspired their harvest traditions?
quote: The Separatists lived in Leiden, Netherlands, from 1609 to 1620, where locals celebrated an annual October 3rd thanksgiving feast commemorating the lifting of the 1574 Spanish siege.

q: Which ship was supposed to sail alongside the Mayflower in 1620, but sprang a leak twice and had to turn back to England, crowding all 102 passengers onto the Mayflower?
quote: The ironically named Speedwell leaked so badly twice that it was left behind in Plymouth, England, delaying the Mayflower's departure until September 1620.

q: Where did the Mayflower first drop anchor in November 1620—where the Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact—before sailing across the bay to Plymouth?
a: Provincetown Harbor at the tip of Cape Cod
quote: The Pilgrims first landed at the tip of Cape Cod (modern-day Provincetown) on November 11, 1620, and spent five weeks exploring before choosing Plymouth.

q: Who was the longtime governor of Plymouth Colony whose handwritten history, 'Of Plimoth Plantation,' was lost during the Revolutionary War and rediscovered in a London bishop's library in 1855?
quote: William Bradford's manuscript was missing for over 70 years until it was found in Fulham Palace in London in 1855, reviving national interest in the 1621 Plymouth story!

q: Two years before the Mayflower landed, on December 4, 1619, English settlers stepped ashore at Berkeley Hundred along the James River and held a service of thanksgiving in which colony?
quote: The 1619 Berkeley Plantation charter in Virginia declared that the day of their ship's arrival 'shall be yearly and perpetually kept holy as a day of thanksgiving'!

q: Spanish explorer Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and members of the Timucua tribe shared a feast of salted pork, garbanzo beans, and red wine after a Mass of Thanksgiving on September 8, 1565, in which modern U.S. city?
quote: Historians point to St. Augustine, Florida—founded 56 years before the Plymouth feast—as the site of the earliest documented European-Native American thanksgiving meal in what is now the United States.

q: In what year did President George Washington issue the very first Presidential Thanksgiving Proclamation by the new U.S. federal government?
quote: On October 3, 1789, George Washington proclaimed Thursday, November 26, 1789, as a national day of public thanksgiving and prayer in honor of the new U.S. Constitution.

q: Which U.S. President refused to issue any Thanksgiving proclamations during his presidency because he believed the Constitution built a 'wall of separation between Church and State'?
quote: Thomas Jefferson felt that proclaiming national days of fasting or thanksgiving was a religious matter best left to individual states and citizens.

q: Which influential 19th-century women's magazine did Sarah Josepha Hale edit for 40 years while publishing yearly editorials and recipes campaigning for a national Thanksgiving holiday?
quote: As editor of 'Godey's Lady's Book'—the most widely read magazine in pre-Civil War America—Sarah Josepha Hale popularized roast turkey and pumpkin pie as standard Thanksgiving fare.

q: Which major Civil War Union victory in July 1863—followed by his famous November address there—helped inspire President Abraham Lincoln to proclaim a national Thanksgiving holiday in October 1863?
quote: Written by Secretary of State William Seward and signed by Lincoln on October 3, 1863, the proclamation urged Americans to 'heal the wounds of the nation' on the final Thursday of November.

q: When Congress passed a joint resolution in December 1941 to end the 'Franksgiving' confusion once and for all, which day did it legally lock in as Thanksgiving Day?
quote: Because November sometimes has five Thursdays, Congress specified the FOURTH Thursday of November so the date never lands as late as November 29 or 30.

q: In 1970, Wampanoag leader Wamsutta (Frank) James established a solemn annual gathering on Cole's Hill overlooking Plymouth Rock on Thanksgiving Day known by what name?
quote: Every Thanksgiving since 1970, Indigenous people and allies have gathered at Cole's Hill in Plymouth for the National Day of Mourning to honor Native ancestors and resilience.

q: How did a bird native exclusively to North and Central America end up being called a 'turkey' in English?
a: Its gobble sounded like the Turkish word for 'hello'
The first European turkey farm was built in Istanbul
16th-century English buyers confused it with guinea fowl imported through Constantinople by Levant ('Turkey') merchants
Christopher Columbus thought he had landed in the Ottoman Empire
quote: When Spanish explorers brought domesticated Aztec turkeys to Europe, English traders lumped them together with exotic 'turkey-cocks' (guinea fowl) shipped by Ottoman Levant merchants!

q: Which ancient Mesoamerican civilization was the first to domesticate the wild turkey more than 2,000 years ago?
a: The Maya and Aztecs of Mexico and Central America
quote: Archaeological evidence shows indigenous peoples of south-central Mexico domesticated turkeys around 800 B.C.–200 B.C., centuries before Europeans arrived.

q: Which U.S. state raises the most turkeys every year—producing roughly 38 to 40 million birds annually?
quote: Minnesota is America's #1 turkey-producing state, followed closely by North Carolina, Arkansas, and Indiana!

q: What are baby turkeys officially called during their first few weeks of life?
quote: Baby turkeys are called poults! For the first month of life, they feed mostly on insects and berries before switching to seeds and acorns.

q: What can the bare skin on a live wild turkey's head and neck do in seconds when the bird gets excited, scared, or ready to court?
a: Inflate to the size of a basketball
Change color between bright red, white, and vivid blue
quote: As blood vessels dilate or constrict, a turkey's bare head can shift between patriotic red, white, and blue in just a few seconds!

q: Where do wild turkeys sleep at night to stay safe from coyotes, foxes, and bobcats?
a: Floating on the middle of ponds
quote: At dusk, wild turkeys fly up into high tree branches to roost for the night, descending back to the ground at dawn.

q: What is the bristle-like tuft of modified feathers sticking out from the center of a male wild turkey's chest called?
quote: It's called a beard! A tom turkey's beard grows continuously about 3 to 5 inches per year (and about 10% of female hens grow one too).

q: Roughly how many feathers does a fully grown adult turkey have covering its body?
quote: An adult turkey has between 5,000 and 6,000 feathers! Only male toms fan their 18 large tail feathers into a full wheel to show off.

q: Which two senses are strongest in a turkey (while its sense of smell is quite poor)?
quote: Because a turkey's eyes are on the sides of its head, it has a 270-degree field of color vision—and even though it has no external ear flaps, it can pinpoint a sound a mile away!

q: Who was the young boy in 1863 who begged his father—President Abraham Lincoln—to spare a live turkey named Jack that had been sent to the White House for Christmas dinner?
quote: Ten-year-old Tad Lincoln adopted the turkey as a pet named Jack, and Lincoln wrote out a reprieve on a card so Jack wouldn't be cooked!

q: In November 1963, President John F. Kennedy spared a 55-pound White House gift turkey wearing a sign around its neck that read what?
quote: Looking at the huge bird wearing a 'Good Eating, Mr. President!' banner on November 19, 1963, JFK smiled and said, 'We'll just let this one grow.'

q: Under the modern White House turkey pardon tradition, how many turkeys travel to Washington, D.C., each November—and why?
a: Twelve turkeys representing the 12 months of the year
Fifty turkeys—one from every U.S. state
Two turkeys (a primary bird and an official alternate) in case one gets stage fright or falls ill
quote: Two turkeys are raised and trained with music and camera flashes to handle the Rose Garden crowd—and both the official bird and its alternate receive a presidential pardon!

q: What were the rhyming names of the pair of White House turkeys pardoned in 2014 that became an instant social media joke?
quote: Over the years, pardoned White House turkey pairs have included Mac and Cheese (2014), Tater and Tot (2016), Bread and Butter (2019), Peanut Butter and Jelly (2021), and Liberty and Bell (2023)!

q: Which turkey bone is dried and pulled apart by two people after Thanksgiving dinner to see who gets the bigger half ('the lucky break')?
quote: The wishbone is the furcula—two fused collarbones that give birds springy strength for flapping their wings. The wish-snapping custom dates back to ancient Etruscans and Romans!

q: In a traditional farmyard turkey, roughly what percentage of the bird's meat is white meat versus dark meat?
a: About 70% white meat and 30% dark meat
quote: A typical Thanksgiving turkey yields roughly 70% white meat (breast and wings) and 30% dark meat (thighs and drumsticks, which have more myoglobin from walking).

q: Approximately how many turkeys are prepared for Thanksgiving across the United States each year?
quote: According to the National Turkey Federation, Americans cook roughly 46 million turkeys for Thanksgiving each year (plus another 22 million at Christmas)!

q: Why did the Butterball Turkey Co. originally establish the 'Turkey Talk-Line' (1-800-BUTTERBALL) in November 1981?
a: To run a national turkey-calling contest
To take complaints about broken oven thermometers
Six home economists answered 11,000 live phone calls from nervous home cooks asking how to thaw and roast a turkey
To sell mail-order stuffing mixes over the phone
quote: Started with 6 home economists in 1981, the Butterball Turkey Talk-Line now fields over 100,000 questions every November and December via phone, text, and voice assistants!

q: According to USDA food-safety guidelines, how long does it take to safely thaw a frozen 16-pound turkey in the refrigerator?
a: About 4 days (24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds)
quote: The USDA's golden rule is 24 hours of refrigerator thawing for every 4 to 5 pounds of turkey—meaning a 16-pound bird needs about 4 full days in the fridge!

q: What is the USDA-recommended minimum internal temperature for a fully cooked Thanksgiving turkey (measured in the thickest part of the breast, thigh, and stuffing)?
quote: Food safety experts confirm a turkey (and any stuffing cooked inside the cavity) is safely cooked when a meat thermometer reaches 165°F.

q: What culinary difference separates 'stuffing' from 'dressing' on a Thanksgiving menu—even though region often determines which word families use?
a: Stuffing uses wheat bread, while dressing only uses rice
Stuffing is cooked inside the turkey cavity, while dressing is baked in a separate pan or casserole dish
Stuffing contains meat, while dressing is strictly vegetarian
Stuffing is served cold, while dressing is served hot
quote: Technically, stuffing is stuffed inside the bird while dressing is baked in a separate dish—though in the American South, 'cornbread dressing' is the universal name either way!

q: Which company introduced Stove Top Stuffing in 1972—invented by home economist Ruth Siems—promising delicious stuffing in 5 minutes without a turkey?
quote: General Foods home economist Ruth Siems patented the exact size and crumb texture of bread cubes so Stove Top Stuffing could rehydrate in a saucepan in just five minutes!

q: Which state produces roughly 85% of all the canned pumpkin sold in the United States—and declared pumpkin pie its official state pie in 2015?
quote: Illinois grows more pumpkins than any other state by far—and the town of Morton, Illinois (home to the Libby's cannery), calls itself the 'Pumpkin Capital of the World'!

q: What variety of squash is actually inside a can of 100% Pure Pumpkin (such as Libby's) rather than an orange Halloween carving jack-o'-lantern?
a: The Dickinson pumpkin (a tan, sweet, dense squash closely related to butternut squash)
Watermelon rind mixed with sweet potato
quote: Carving jack-o'-lanterns are stringy and watery, so canneries use the tan-skinned Dickinson cultivar of Cucurbita moschata, prized for its creamy, sweet orange flesh!

q: How do farmers harvest wet-harvested cranberries in Massachusetts and Wisconsin every autumn?
a: Drain the lakes completely and dig the roots up like potatoes
Send trained diving dogs into the ponds
Wait for the bogs to freeze solid and vacuum the berries off the ice
They flood the bogs with water, use water reels to knock the floating berries loose, and corral them
quote: Cranberries don't actually grow underwater! They grow on dry low vines in sandy beds, and farmers flood the bogs the night before harvest because air pockets inside the berries make them float.

q: Who was the Massachusetts lawyer and cranberry grower who first boiled damaged cranberries with sugar and water in 1912 and canned them—founding the cooperative that became Ocean Spray?
quote: Marcus Urann wanted a way to make the short six-week autumn cranberry crop available year-round—and today millions of families serve jellied cranberry sauce ridges and all!

q: Why are the orange-fleshed tubers in a Thanksgiving casserole almost always 'sweet potatoes' in U.S. grocery stores, even when the can or recipe calls them 'candied yams'?
a: True yams are rough-skinned tropical tubers native to Africa and Asia, while soft orange U.S. varieties are sweet potatoes
A sweet potato turns into a yam once marshmallows are melted on top
'Yam' is just the French word for baked potato
Yams and sweet potatoes are the exact same plant picked in different months
quote: In the 1930s, Louisiana growers marketed their soft, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes as 'yams' (from the West African word 'nyami') to distinguish them from firmer, pale-fleshed northern sweet potatoes.

q: In what decade did a booklet commissioned by angel-food cake and marshmallow makers first popularize topping Thanksgiving sweet potatoes with toasted marshmallows?
quote: In 1917, the Angelus Marshmallow company hired Boston Cooking School Magazine founder Janet McKenzie Hill to create home recipes using mass-produced marshmallows—and sweet potato casserole with marshmallows was born!

q: Which crunchy, nutty pie—made with corn syrup, eggs, butter, sugar, and native tree nuts—became a Thanksgiving staple across the American South in the 1920s and 1930s after Karo syrup printed the recipe on its labels?
quote: Pecans are the only major tree nut native to North America, and the sales manager's wife at Karo Corn Syrup popularized the modern pecan pie recipe in the 1930s!

q: What are the 'giblets' often found tucked inside a paper or plastic pouch inside a store-bought whole turkey?
a: The heart, gizzard, liver, and neck (often simmered to make rich turkey gravy or stuffing stock)
Extra packets of sage and thyme
quote: Many a rookie Thanksgiving cook has accidentally roasted the little giblet bag still tucked inside the turkey's neck or body cavity!

q: Which culinary technique—wrapping or tying a turkey's legs and wings close to its body with kitchen twine—helps the bird roast evenly without drying out the breast?
quote: Trussing pulls the wings and drumsticks snug against the body so the extremities don't overcook before the thickest part of the turkey reaches 165°F.

q: Which Thanksgiving turkey cooking method—cutting out the backbone and pressing the bird flat so it roasts in nearly half the time with crispy skin all over—has become a favorite of modern chefs?
quote: Spatchcocking a turkey exposes the dark-meat thighs to higher direct heat so the thighs and breast finish cooking at the exact same time!

q: According to the National Fire Protection Association, Thanksgiving Day has more than triple the daily average of home cooking fires—most often caused by what backyard cooking mishap?
a: Boiling cranberries on a camp stove
Dropping a partially frozen or wet turkey into an overfilled outdoor propane deep-fryer
Warming dinner rolls in a toaster
quote: When ice or water inside a turkey hits 350°F peanut oil, it instantly flashes to steam and expands 1,700 times in volume, causing boiling oil to spill over the pot onto the burner flame!

q: According to nutrition researchers at the Calorie Control Council, roughly how many calories does the average American consume during a full Thanksgiving dinner (including appetizers, sides, drinks, and dessert)?
quote: Between buttery mashed potatoes, stuffing, gravy, pie, and seconds, a full Thanksgiving feast plus nibbles can easily top 3,000 to 4,500 calories!

q: Which famous guest always closes out the finale of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in Herald Square, officially kicking off the holiday season?
a: The Mayor of New York riding a giant turkey
Santa Claus on his sleigh float
quote: Santa Claus has closed out every Macy's Parade since the very first one in 1924 (except 1933, when he led the parade at the very front)!

q: Who was the theatrical puppeteer and designer who invented the first giant character balloons for the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1927?
quote: Master puppeteer Tony Sarg designed upside-down marionettes filled with air and helium in partnership with the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company in Akron, Ohio!

q: Between 1928 and 1932, how did Macy's dispose of its giant parade balloons at the end of the parade—until a pilot nearly crashed trying to catch one?
a: They donated them to the circus as tents
They popped them with pins in Central Park
They floated them across the Hudson River on barges
They released them into the sky to float away for days, offering a $100 reward to anyone who mailed a deflated balloon back
quote: For five years Macy's let the balloons drift away with return-address labels attached—until 1932, when a student pilot flew into a drifting Tom Cat balloon over Queens and barely escaped!

q: Why was the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade canceled for three straight years in 1942, 1943, and 1944?
a: Macy's flagship store was being rebuilt
World War II shortages—Macy's deflated and donated 650 pounds of balloon rubber to the U.S. military war effort
quote: During World War II, helium and rubber were vital military supplies. Macy's ceremonial deflation of a giant dragon balloon yielded 650 pounds of scrap rubber for the armed forces!

q: Which iconic float has led the front of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade almost every year since 1979?
a: Tom Turkey (the giant head-bobbing, wing-flapping turkey float)
quote: Tom Turkey is the official mascot and lead float of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, greeting millions of spectators at the start of the 2.5-mile Manhattan route!

q: What is the oldest Thanksgiving Day parade in the United States—founded in 1920, four years before Macy's first parade?
a: Philadelphia's Thanksgiving Day Parade (originally the Gimbel Brothers Parade)
quote: Department store rival Gimbel Brothers launched the first Thanksgiving parade in Philadelphia in 1920 with 50 people, 15 cars, and a fireman dressed as Santa!

q: What marches down the streets of Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 'America's Hometown Thanksgiving Parade' instead of fictional cartoon balloons?
a: Floats made entirely out of cranberries
Chronological historical units, drum corps, and living-history reenactors portraying four centuries of American history
quote: Plymouth's parade arranges its floats and marchers strictly in chronological order from the 17th-century Pilgrims and Wampanoag through the 20th century!

q: What is the oldest continuously run footrace in North America—held every Thanksgiving morning since 1896 when six runners raced 5 miles down dirt roads?
a: The Buffalo YMCA Turkey Trot in Buffalo, New York
quote: Founded on Thanksgiving 1896 with just six runners, the Buffalo YMCA Turkey Trot is the oldest consecutively run footrace in North America (even older than the 1897 Boston Marathon)!

q: Why did Detroit Lions owner George A. Richards originally schedule a Thanksgiving Day home football game in 1934?
a: Because the Detroit Tigers baseball team was using the field on Sunday
Because the stadium lights were broken for night games
As a marketing stunt to pack the stadium and broadcast the game coast-to-coast on his 94-station NBC radio network
quote: Richards owned radio station WJR and convinced NBC to air the Lions vs. undefeated Chicago Bears live on Thanksgiving 1934—selling out all 26,000 seats and launching an annual tradition!

q: Since 2006, the NFL has played how many Thanksgiving Day football games each year (afternoon in Detroit, late afternoon in Dallas, plus an evening matchup)?
quote: In 2006, the NFL added a third prime-time night game (now honoring the John Madden Thanksgiving Celebration) alongside the classic Detroit Lions and Dallas Cowboys afternoon games.

q: What is the name of the playful Thanksgiving Day matchup featuring rescue puppies and senior dogs shown alongside the National Dog Show?
a: The National Dog Show (hosted by the Kennel Club of Philadelphia right after the Macy's Parade)
quote: Since 2002, over 20 million viewers have tuned in right after the Macy's Parade on NBC to watch the Kennel Club of Philadelphia's National Dog Show!

q: In the freak 1993 Thanksgiving snow-and-sleet game between the Miami Dolphins and Dallas Cowboys, whose last-second blunder on a blocked field goal allowed Miami to kick a winning retry?
a: Cowboys defensive lineman Leon Lett, who slid into the live football on the snowy turf
quote: Dallas had blocked Miami's game-winning field goal in the snow and only needed to stay away from the ball—but Leon Lett tried to recover it, slipped, and touched it, giving Miami possession at the 1-yard line!

q: In the 1998 Thanksgiving overtime coin toss in Detroit, Steelers running back Jerome Bettis swore he called 'tails,' while referee Phil Luckett heard 'heads-tails' and awarded the ball to Detroit—prompting what NFL rule change?
a: Captains must now state their coin-toss call BEFORE the referee flips the coin into the air
Overtime games are decided by a field-goal contest instead of a coin toss
Coaches flip the coin themselves on the sideline
Thanksgiving games can no longer go to overtime
quote: After the infamous 'Heels/Heads-Tails' Thanksgiving coin-toss controversy, the NFL changed its rulebook so the visiting captain calls heads or tails before the coin leaves the referee's thumb!

q: Which two college football programs first met on Thanksgiving Day in 1876 in Hoboken, New Jersey, starting a 19th-century holiday college football craze that predated the NFL by 58 years?
quote: Yale and Princeton played their first Thanksgiving championship game in 1876—by the 1890s, over 40,000 fans packed Manhattan's Polo Grounds every Thanksgiving to watch!

q: In the famous 1947 holiday movie that begins during the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, an actor hired to play Santa Claus insists he is the real Kris Kringle. What is the film's title?
quote: The opening scenes of 'Miracle on 34th Street' were filmed live during the actual 1946 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City, with star Edmund Gwenn riding the real Santa float!

q: Which beloved 1987 comedy stars Steve Martin and John Candy as two mismatched travelers trying to get home to Chicago for Thanksgiving dinner by train, bus, and burned-out rental car?
quote: John Hughes wrote 'Planes, Trains and Automobiles' after his own real-life nightmare flight from New York to Chicago was diverted to Wichita and took three days!

q: In the classic 1978 Thanksgiving episode of the sitcom 'WKRP in Cincinnati' ('Turkeys Away'), what happens when station manager Arthur Carlson drops live turkeys from a helicopter as a promotion?
a: The turkeys land peacefully on the mayor's roof
A hawk chases the helicopter back to the airport
The domestic turkeys can't fly and plummet into the shopping center parking lot, prompting the line: 'As God is my witness, I thought turkeys could fly!'
The turkeys fly away to Florida with the station's banner
quote: Based on a real 1950s Dallas radio station promotion (where turkeys were tossed from a truck), 'Turkeys Away' was named by TV Guide as one of the greatest sitcom episodes in television history!

q: On the TV show 'Friends,' which character famously puts a whole raw Thanksgiving turkey over their head (complete with sunglasses and a fez) to cheer up Chandler?
a: Monica Geller (after Joey did it first to scare Chandler)
quote: In Season 5's 'The One with All the Thanksgivings,' Joey gets his head stuck inside a 19-pound turkey first, and Monica later puts it on with a fez and sunglasses—making Chandler blurt out 'I love you' for the first time!

q: In another famous 'Friends' Thanksgiving episode, why does Rachel's homemade English trifle taste like 'feet' to Ross?
a: Two cookbook pages stuck together, so she layered ladyfingers, custard, and jam with beef sautéed with peas and onions
She accidentally used salt instead of powdered sugar
She baked it with garlic butter instead of vanilla
She dropped the bowl on the apartment carpet
quote: Half English trifle and half shepherd's pie—only Joey EATS every bite and declares: 'Custard? Good. Jam? Good. Meat? Goooood!'

q: Which comedic 1990s singer performed 'The Thanksgiving Song' on Saturday Night Live's Weekend Update ('Turkey for me, turkey for you, let's eat the turkey in my big brown shoe')?
quote: Adam Sandler debuted 'The Thanksgiving Song' on SNL in November 1992 after realizing radio stations had hundreds of Christmas songs but almost no funny Thanksgiving songs!

q: Folk singer Arlo Guthrie's 18-minute talking-blues anthem 'Alice's Restaurant Massacree'—played by rock radio stations every Thanksgiving since 1967—begins with what real-life Thanksgiving Day misadventure?
a: Losing a pet turkey on the New York Thruway
Getting arrested in Stockbridge, Massachusetts, for littering after finding the town dump closed on Thanksgiving
Burning down Alice's restaurant kitchen with a deep-fryer
Getting snowed in at a roadside diner for a week
quote: On Thanksgiving 1965, 18-year-old Arlo Guthrie and a friend tried to haul out Alice Brock's church-home trash in a VW microbus, leading to the famous 'twenty-seven 8-by-10 color glossy pictures with circles and arrows'!

q: What was the title of the 2013 animated comedy film in which two turkeys named Reggie and Jake (voiced by Owen Wilson and Woody Harrelson) use a time machine to travel back to 1621 to get turkeys off the Thanksgiving menu?
quote: In 'Free Birds' (2013), the time-traveling turkeys replace turkey at the 1621 Plymouth feast with delivery pizza from Chuck E. Cheese!

q: In 1578—43 years before the Plymouth feast—English explorer Martin Frobisher held the first recorded European Thanksgiving ceremony in North America after surviving icy waters in what is now which territory?
a: Nunavut, Canada (Frobisher Bay on Baffin Island)
quote: Frobisher and his crew gave formal thanks on Baffin Island in 1578 with a communion service and a meal of salt beef, biscuits, and mushy peas—the historical root of Canadian Thanksgiving!

q: Which West African nation—founded in the 19th century by freed African Americans—celebrates a national Thanksgiving Day on the first Thursday of November with concerts and roasted chicken or mashed cassavas?
quote: Liberia established its national Thanksgiving Day in the 1880s on the first Thursday of November, blending American harvest traditions with vibrant West African music and spicy dishes!

q: On tiny Norfolk Island (an Australian territory in the South Pacific), why do residents celebrate American Thanksgiving on the last Wednesday of November with cornbread and pumpkin pie?
a: 19th-century American whaling ships and traders brought the holiday to the island in the 1890s
The Mayflower stopped there on a world tour
It marks the island's volcano harvest day
Wild turkeys swim to the island every November
quote: American trader Isaac Robinson decorated Norfolk Island's All Saints Church with palm leaves and cornstalks for Thanksgiving in the 1890s, and islanders have celebrated it ever since!

q: In the Dutch city of Leiden—where the Pilgrims lived before sailing on the Mayflower—which historic church still holds an annual non-denominational American Thanksgiving Day service every November?
a: The Pieterskerk (St. Peter's Church, where Pilgrim pastor John Robinson is buried)
quote: Every fourth Thursday of November, the 900-year-old Pieterskerk in Leiden hosts an annual Thanksgiving Day service honoring the hospitality shown to the Pilgrims in the 1600s.

q: What name did the National Retail Federation coin in 2005 for the Monday after Thanksgiving weekend, when millions of workers returned to their office computers to shop online?
quote: Ellen Davis and Scott Silverman at Shop.org coined 'Cyber Monday' in a 2005 press release after noticing online retail traffic spiked every Monday after Thanksgiving when people used fast office internet connections!
